Alternate Name: Dhammachakra Anuvartan Din; Dhammachakra Anuvartan Diwas; Ashoka Vijayadashami
Category: Buddhist Religious Festival / Mass Conversion Commemoration
Deity: Gautama Buddha; Dr. B. R. Ambedkar is honoured
Historical Background: Commemorates Dr. B. R. Ambedkar and approximately half a million followers embracing Buddhism at Deekshabhoomi, Nagpur, on 14 October 1956. Further conversions took place in the following days.
Rituals: Buddhist prayers, homage to Buddha, recitation of the Three Refuges, Five Precepts and Ambedkar's 22 vows, speeches and conversion ceremonies
Fair Activities: Religious gatherings, speeches, book stalls, community meetings and conversion ceremonies at Deekshabhoomi
Cultural Significance: Commemorates Ambedkar's mass conversion to Buddhism and symbolises equality, dignity, liberty and opposition to caste discrimination. It also celebrates the revival of Buddhism in India.

Historical Background: Worship and processions
Rituals: N/A
Fair Activities: Traditional performances reportedly declined from audiences of thousands to a few hundred in some cases.
Cultural Significance: N/A

Duration: Several days or nights, depending on the occasion and local performance
Historical Background: Dandar is a folk theatre and dance tradition associated with Gond, Korku and Pardhi communities. It is connected with religious occasions, harvest time and village celebrations. The form combines music, dance, theatrical performance and storytelling and is linked to the development of Zadipatti theatre. Younger participation is declining due to migration and changing entertainment preferences.
Rituals: Music, dance, theatrical performance and storytelling.
Fair Activities: Festival programmes, village performances and open-field performances.
Cultural Significance: Important Gond, Korku and Pardhi folk tradition connected with the development of Zadipatti theatre.

Historical Background: Gal Utsav has been associated with Kondhala for more than three generations. The Kondhala fair is reported to have continued for over 200 years, and worship at Mahadevji Burade’s home has continued since his great-grandfather’s time. An earlier celebration involved bringing a tall mahua wooden pole into the village using bullock carts; this was later replaced by a permanent concrete structure.
Rituals: Procession carrying a box associated with local deities, accompanied by traditional percussion; religious worship; use of a horizontal beam and long rope at the festival site
Fair Activities: Shops, vendors, toys, household goods and food stalls; theatrical performances and a Tamasha programme
Cultural Significance: A religious and community gathering that preserves local worship traditions, supports folk arts and entertainment, and brings together surrounding villages.

Historical Background: The three-day Mahalakshmi Puja is an important part of the ten-day Ganesh festival in Vidarbha. Traditionally, extended families gathered a day or two before the puja, and women prepared fulora, prasad, ambil and a large ritual meal together. Smaller family units and changing lifestyles have increased reliance on caterers, reducing collective preparation and knowledge of traditional cooking and serving methods.
Rituals: Invocation (aavahan) under Aniruddha Nakshatra; worship under Jyeshtha Nakshatra; immersion (visarjan) under Mool Nakshatra; household puja; dressing the goddesses; preparing fulora and prasad; serving the ritual meal; washing hands at a designated pit, according to the source
Fair Activities: Family gatherings, preparing and serving the ritual meal, and feeding people during the puja
Cultural Significance: Preserves household worship, traditional culinary knowledge, ritual serving practices and family customs. Although social gatherings remain significant, collective preparation of elaborate meals has reduced in some households.

Deity: Karam Devta or Karamsani, associated with strength, youth and vitality
Duration: 1 main day (Karam Ekadashi, Bhado/Bhadrapada Shukla 11); preparations begin about 10–12 days earlier
Historical Background: A tribal harvest festival centred on the sacred Karam tree, traditionally regarded as a symbol of Karam Devta or Karamsani. The festival is celebrated by tribal populations in several Indian states and is particularly associated with Munda, Ho, Oraon, Baiga, Kharia and Santhal communities. In Vidarbha, associated traditions include Gond and Korku communities. Migration from villages to cities, shrinking community spaces, changing entertainment preferences and weakening intergenerational cultural transmission have contributed to declining participation in traditional dance forms.
Rituals: Worship around the sacred Karam tree; communal Karma dance accompanied by the timki. The dance is associated with religious and seasonal occasions, agricultural cycles and community gatherings.
Fair Activities: Karma dance and community gatherings
Cultural Significance: Connects tribal religious beliefs with harvest practices and community identity. The Karam tree symbolises strength, youth and vitality. The associated dance preserves traditional movements, music and rhythms, but declining participation threatens the transmission of this cultural knowledge to younger generations.

Village: Surjagad hills, Etapalli taluka; fair held at the Thakurdev temple just before Surjagad village, with the hill about 2 km behind it
Deity: Thakur Dev (idol mounted on a horse in the temple)
Duration: 3–4 days, depending on the year and source
Historical Background: Principal festival of the tribal people of Gadchiroli and neighbouring districts; combines religious devotion with remembrance of the anti-British struggle
Rituals: Devotees pay obeisance to Thakur Dev; local accounts say the climb to the top of the fort takes 3–4 hours
Fair Activities: Not confirmed in sources
Cultural Significance: Major festival for the Madia tribes of Bhamragad and Etapalli talukas

Village: Bejur village, Bhamragad tehsil. It is 8 km from Bhamragad and 182 km from Gadchiroli.
Deity: Bablai Mata (Bablai Devi), presiding deity of Adivasis across the Bhamragad region
Historical Background: The site is seen as a protective space for local tribal groups, and oral tradition holds that Bablai Devi safeguards the surrounding forests and communities. It is described as a living symbol of cultural, environmental and constitutional rights.
Rituals: Collective worship. Villagers clean sacred groves, and about 22 traditional office-bearers manage the worship and the yatra. A traditional convention is held where gram sabhas discuss the Forest Rights Act and PESA. Devotees also trek up hilltops to worship.
Fair Activities: Rela dance performed by village groups, and people singing and dancing together at night. The Bablai story is passed down orally, not in writing.
Cultural Significance: Annual renewal of generations-old culture, traditions and relationship with nature. Gotul samitis plan it every year.

Historical Background: Sacred hill-site gathering where approximately 40 villages assemble; demonstrates the role of natural landscapes as sacred spaces.
Rituals: Ritual worship, collective prayers and offerings to deities.
Fair Activities: Community celebration and exchange of traditions
Cultural Significance: Strengthens ties among villages and sustains shared tribal traditions within the regional ritual calendar.

Historical Background: Sacred river-ghat gathering where approximately 33 villages participate; illustrates the integration of natural landscapes into tribal religious systems.
Rituals: Ritual worship and collective prayers.
Fair Activities: Community gathering and exchange of traditions
Cultural Significance: Reinforces communal solidarity and demonstrates the connection between tribal identity, geography and annual ritual traditions.

Historical Background: Organized in honor of Sanskrit poet Kalidas; associated with Vidarbha's cultural heritage

Fair Activities: Darshan at Sant Bhojaji Maharaj’s Samadhi, devotional worship, offering Puranpoli as naivedya, receiving Puranpoli prasad, and community meals (Mahaprasad).
Cultural Significance: Devotional significance

Historical Background: Celebrates Krishna and Rukmini's sacred marital union
Rituals: Religious gathering
Fair Activities: Temple worship, aarti, devotional bhajans, palkhi procession, Dahi Handi celebrations, and distribution of Mahaprasad.
Cultural Significance: Religious heritage

Rituals: Creation of Kala Marbat and Pivli Marbat effigies; processions; chanting slogans; ritual burning or immersion of effigies; community participation
Fair Activities: Processions, traditional music, drumming, folk performances, street plays and cultural activities
Cultural Significance: Symbolically represents the destruction of evil and negativity and provides a platform for social expression and community participation

Historical Background: Traditional folk practice during Navratri
Rituals: Singing traditional melodies and dancing

Cultural Significance: Sisterhood and regional folk tradition

Alternate Name: Ramtek Adventure and Heritage Tourism Festival

Fair Activities: Heritage walk, bird watching, cultural events, competitions, bullock and tractor rides
Cultural Significance: Combines religious celebration with heritage, cultural and adventure activities

Historical Background: Temple dedicated to goddess Durga incarnation on Korambhi hill
Rituals: Maha Aarti and prayers
Fair Activities: Yatra, shopping, boating and temple visit
Cultural Significance: Religious importance of the hill temple and Navratri tradition

Rituals: Hanuman Chalisa reading, red tilak, vermillion with ghee, fasting and worship

Cultural Significance: Religious importance of the ancient Shiva shrine and sacred landscape

Cultural Significance: Local Mahashivratri pilgrimage and community tradition

Historical Background: Celebrates Lord Shiva's victory over demon Tripurasara
Rituals: Maha Puja, holy bath and worship
Fair Activities: Folk dance and cultural performances
Cultural Significance: Combines Shiva worship with classical and folk arts

Rituals: Puja and fasting; Ras Garba

Historical Background: Utsav describes the temple as an ancient temple and the idol as swayambhu according to local belief

Festival Name: Shri Kshetra Jalicha Dev Chakradhar Swami Buldhana Yatra
Historical Background: Pilgrimage associated with Shri Chakradhar Swami and the Mahanubhava Panth
Rituals: Palakhi procession; bhajan; kirtan; Maha Aarti; Maha Prasad
Fair Activities: Mass rally, procession, stalls, pravachan
Cultural Significance: Important pilgrimage site for followers of the Mahanubhava tradition

Historical Background: Annual yatra at Gadge Maharaj Samadhi Temple commemorating his social work
Rituals: Temple visit; cleanliness drive; procession
Fair Activities: Jatra, songs, dances, amusement activities

Historical Background: Commemorates the saint's first appearance at Shegaon
Rituals: Religious observances and pilgrimage
Fair Activities: Food, lodging and pilgrimage arrangements
Cultural Significance: Important pilgrimage and religious gathering in Buldhana district

Rituals: Shobha Yatra, burning of old clothes and cotton wicks, lighting of Tipur flame, Mandai cultural programme
Fair Activities: Fair, cultural tableaux, folk performances, wrestling and entertainment

Historical Background: The tradition began in 1787 during the period of Shrimant Raje Khandhoji Maharaj Bhosale (Chimanabapu). A Ganpati idol was installed during Pitru Paksha after the regular Ganpati festival had concluded, in connection with his return to Nagpur after a victorious Bengal campaign.
Rituals: Ganpati installation during Pitru Paksha and religious observances
Fair Activities: Khadi Gammat, Nakla, Lavani, Bhajan, Powada and other folk-art performances
Cultural Significance: The festival combines Ganpati worship with Bhosale-era history and Nagpur's local folk-art traditions.

Historical Background: The yatra is associated with a cave Shiv Mandir containing a self-manifested Shivling. Local traditions connect the site with Rishi Dhaumya and Sant Harihar Baba, who meditated in nearby forests for 12 years.
Rituals: Cave temple worship; devotees enter one at a time; tying cloth to Peepal tree as a vow
Fair Activities: Teerthayatra and devotional gathering
Cultural Significance: Preserves local Shaiva traditions and the spiritual significance associated with the cave temple.

Historical Background: Annual festival dedicated to Bhagwan Khandoba, who is associated with warrior traditions and pastoral communities.
Rituals: Rath procession carrying the murti of Khandoba; bhajans, kirtans and offerings
Fair Activities: Rath/chariot procession, bhajans and kirtans
Cultural Significance: Reflects devotional traditions associated with Khandoba and communal worship in the village.

Historical Background: Celebrated in memory of Sant Nanaji Maharaj. The Laxmi Narayan Mandir was constructed by Nanaji Maharaj in 1890 with local villagers. His and his wife's samadhi are located near the temple.
Rituals: Aarti, bhajans, Mahanaivedya, Dahi Handi during Rath Saptami, prayers and community meals
Fair Activities: Dahi Handi, cultural programs, bhajans, community meal/Anna Chhatra
Cultural Significance: Represents Vidarbha's saint tradition and deep-rooted devotional culture.

Historical Background: The yatra is centered on a 700-year-old murti of Bhagwan Ram in Pavnar.
Rituals: Rath procession from Pavnar to Wardha
Fair Activities: Rath procession
Cultural Significance: Highlights the long-standing religious tradition associated with the ancient Ram murti of Pavnar.

Historical Background: The jatra is one of the largest jatras in Amravati and is held at the Shri Amba Devi Mandir. The murti is described as Swayambhu.
Rituals: Daily puja, Panchamrit prasad, mantra chanting, darshan, bhajan and kirtan
Fair Activities: Cultural programs, bhajan, kirtan and procession
Cultural Significance: Major religious and cultural tradition of Amravati centered on Shri Amba Devi.

Historical Background: Local tradition states that a small murti of Bahiram was discovered on the hill about 500 years ago. The present temple was constructed in 1957 by a devotee from the Mali community.
Rituals: Puja, lighting diyas, vow fulfillment and pilgrimage
Fair Activities: Fair and pilgrimage activities
Cultural Significance: Important pilgrimage tradition centered on Bahiram Hill and local religious customs.

Festival Name: Shah Doula Rahiman Shah Gazi Urus
Historical Background: Commemorates Shah Doula Rahiman Shah Gazi, described as a warrior and martyr. His tomb dates to 1340 CE and became a site of reverence.
Rituals: Washing the tomb with scented water and religious observances
Fair Activities: Wrestling, Qawwali, Tamasha and market stalls
Cultural Significance: Preserves the religious and historical traditions associated with Shah Gazi and Achalpur.

Historical Background: Salbardi is located at the Satpura ranges and is known for a cave associated with Bhagwan Mahadev and a Swayambhu Linga.
Rituals: Cave puja, vows, processions and traditional rituals
Fair Activities: Processions and traditional “Poha” ceremonial pole ritual
Cultural Significance: Important Mahashivratri pilgrimage tradition associated with the natural cave and Swayambhu Linga.

Historical Background: The jatra is associated with Kaudanyapur, traditionally considered the birthplace of Rukhmini Devi.
Rituals: Devotional worship and activities at the temple complex; drum performances at the Nagarkhana
Fair Activities: Jatra activities and Nagarkhana drum performances
Cultural Significance: Connects local religious tradition with the story and worship of Vithal and Rukhmini.

Historical Background: The jatra honors Sant Krishnaji Buwa, also known as Vithal Buwa or Awadhut Buwa, who spent 45 years in meditation at Sawanga Vithoba.
Rituals: Worship at the Sant's mandir and samadhi; devotional observances
Fair Activities: Jatra and pilgrimage activities
Cultural Significance: Preserves the saint tradition and devotional history associated with Sant Krishnaji Buwa.

Historical Background: According to the source's account, a shepherd found a child suffering from boils in the jungle and named him Bendoji. Bendoji later became known for miracles and attracted followers.
Rituals: Worship at Bendoji Baba Mandir and remembrance of the Sant
Fair Activities: Fair and religious activities
Cultural Significance: Significant saint-centered jatra preserving the tradition and memory of Bendoji Baba.

Deity: Meghnath (in villages where Meghnath is worshipped)
Historical Background: Tribal communities of Melghat have followed this Holi tradition for thousands of years. It is described as their biggest annual celebration, comparable to Diwali in urban areas.
Rituals: Holi celebrations, traditional tribal dances and community gatherings
Fair Activities: Tribal dances, music, shopping and community celebrations
Cultural Significance: Important expression of Melghat's tribal cultural identity and community traditions.

Historical Background: Organized by the Sindhi community in Amravati because Kanwar Ram Lord's great-grandsons lived in the city.
Rituals: Bhajan, kirtan, bhandara and community service
Fair Activities: Children's mela, bhajan-kirtan, free medical and health camps
Cultural Significance: Combines Sindhi community traditions, religious remembrance, charity and social welfare activities.

Historical Background: Shri Samarth Ramdas Swami visited Bhandara for Dharma Prachar; a Math was founded in Madhav Nagar containing his Paduka and Jholi
Rituals: Bhajans, kirtans, communal prayers, Palkhi procession carrying the sacred Paduka
Fair Activities: Palkhi procession and devotional programs
Cultural Significance: Preserves the devotional legacy and teachings associated with Shri Samarth Ramdas Swami

Historical Background: Local tradition tells of a devout woman (gaulan) whose devotion to Bhagwan Shiv led to the Shiv Pind breaking open
Rituals: Puja and religious rituals
Fair Activities: Cultural performances; local markets; purchase of math/madaka
Cultural Significance: Important local jatra centered on the gram devta Bahirangeshwar and Bhandara-specific ritual traditions

Historical Background: The yatra has a 150-year tradition and is described as resembling a yatra held in Jagannath Puri
Rituals: Wooden murti of Shrihari Balaji Maharaj is carried on a wooden horse through the villages; procession begins at Swayambhu Hanuman Mandir
Fair Activities: Horse procession; jatra; public viewing of the wooden horse and murti
Cultural Significance: A long-standing regional tradition connecting villages through a distinctive horse procession and fair

Historical Background: Described as a major jatra of Vidarbha and a gathering attended by tribal people from different parts of the country
Rituals: Devotees travel to the Kachargadh caves; homage and rituals are performed at the sacred site.
Fair Activities: Jatra activities and folk-art performances; provides opportunities for artists
Cultural Significance: Helps preserve traditional folk arts and provides livelihood opportunities for artists

Historical Background: Gota Paatana is an annual ritual of the Naroti clan at their sacred Raud sites. It reflects Indigenous clan traditions distinct from conventional Hindu temple practices.
Rituals: Clan members gather at Raud, perform puja and seek blessings for good harvest and clan prosperity; ritual is performed for devtas without an anga
Fair Activities: Clan gathering, social interaction and discussion of clan matters
Cultural Significance: Strengthens clan identity, spiritual relationships, social bonds, agricultural hopes and Indigenous cultural traditions

Historical Background: Organized by the Agricultural Science Center of Sonapur; began in 2018 and promotes local mango varieties, farmers and agricultural development.
Rituals: Display and promotion of mango varieties, agricultural guidance and interaction with farmer producer companies and women's self-help groups
Fair Activities: Mango exhibition, agricultural promotion and interaction with farmers/SHGs
Cultural Significance: Promotes local agricultural biodiversity, mango cultivation, farmer development and women's self-help groups

Historical Background: Celebrated at the ancient Markanda Mandir complex on the Wainganga River. The temple complex is believed to have been built by the Rashtrakuta dynasty between the 8th and 12th centuries.
Rituals: Sacred bath in the Uttaravahini, worship of Bhagwan Markandeshwar and prayers for removal of sins and misfortunes
Fair Activities: Pilgrimage, sacred bathing, temple worship and gathering of devotees
Cultural Significance: Preserves the religious and historical importance of the ancient Markanda temple complex and attracts devotees from the region

Deity: Devi Pranhita; Kaleshwar-Mukteshwar,Shri Vitthal and Rukmai
Historical Background: A large religious gathering held every 12 years on the Pranhita River at Sironcha. It attracts pilgrims from several Indian states and is connected with pilgrimage to Kaleshwaram, known as Dakshina Kashi.
Rituals: Taking a holy dip in the Pranhita River, puja to Devi Pranhita, offering pindas to ancestors, visiting Shri Vitthal and Rukmai, travelling to Kaleshwaram and seeking blessings of Kaleshwar-Mukteshwar
Fair Activities: Pilgrimage, river bathing, worship, ancestor rituals and visits to temples
Cultural Significance: Connects Gadchiroli with an inter-state pilgrimage network and preserves religious traditions associated with the Pranhita River and Kaleshwaram

Village: Chanda Club Ground, Civil Lines, Chandrapur
Historical Background: First held in 2024 in Chandrapur; aimed to showcase Tadoba's success in wildlife protection and highlight local efforts in conservation and community development.
Rituals: N/A
Fair Activities: Presentations by forest experts, scientists, and community members; discussions on tiger conservation challenges and solutions.
Cultural Significance: Provided a platform for dialogue and collaboration on tiger conservation.

Historical Background: The Mahakali Mandir is described as the city's most important religious site. It houses two separate murtis, with the second accessible through an underground passage.
Rituals: Religious ceremonies and practices; singing kirtans; maha aarti; palkhi procession.
Fair Activities: Vendors and shops sell jewelry, toys, household appliances and other items.
Cultural Significance: Described as a much-anticipated annual event among Chandrapur residents.

Duration: One month; starts on 5th of Phalgun and ends on 5th of Chaitra
Historical Background: The mandir was once called the Mandir of Bhadranath, associated with Bhagwaan Shiv. It underwent a period of Buddhist dominance during which cave mandirs were constructed. After Buddhist power was abolished, the original mandir was restored and renamed Bhadranag.
Rituals: Worship and darshan of Bhadranaga
Fair Activities: Religious gatherings and pilgrimage
Cultural Significance: Preserves local religious traditions and attracts devotees from nearby regions

Historical Background: Jogapur is located in the forests of Rajura Taluka and is described as attracting many people from Eastern Vidarbha and Telangana. The Jagapu Devi Mandir is at its center.
Rituals: N/A
Fair Activities: Pilgrimage and visits to Jagapu Devi Mandir
Cultural Significance: Attracts devotees from eastern Vidarbha and Telangana and preserves local religious traditions

Historical Background: The festival observes the death anniversary of spiritual Sadguru Ranganath Baba.
Rituals: Daily bhajan processions, kirtans, sermons, palkhi processions to nearby villages, puja of Sadguru Ranganath Baba's Samadhi, aarti, and curd breaking.
Fair Activities: Grand palkhi ceremony on the last day; warkaris from adjacent villages participate.
Cultural Significance: Spreads Sadguru Ranganath Baba's presence to nearby villages.

Deity: Sant Shri Ghanti Baba; Lord Hanuman is also associated with the nearby temple
Historical Background: Described as one of the most important fairs in Yavatmal District.
Rituals: Daily bhajans and kirtans; a procession carrying Ghanti Baba's photograph
Fair Activities: Traders and shopkeepers set up temporary stalls; agricultural produce and articles of daily use are brought for sale.
Cultural Significance: Described as one of the most important fairs in the district.

Historical Background: Famous temple of Shri Ranganath Swami is located in Wani.
Rituals: Preserves local devotional traditions and the historic cattle-trading economy of the Vidarbha region
Fair Activities: Temporary stalls; sale of agricultural produce and daily-use articles; trade in bullocks and other cattle.
Cultural Significance: Described as one of the most important fairs; the fair is famous for trade in bullock and other cattle.

Historical Background: Kalamb is an ancient village. There is a typical underground temple dedicated to Chintamani and a famous water tank known as Ganesh Kunda.
Rituals: Temple worship, darshan, and ritual bathing in the sacred Ganesh Kund
Fair Activities: Temporary stalls; agricultural produce and daily-use articles are brought for sale.
Cultural Significance: Described as an important fair associated with the underground temple dedicated to Chintamani.

Duration: About one month (main day: Dahi Handi)
Historical Background: Listed among the other important fairs of Yavatmal District.
Rituals: Devotional worship and Dahi Handi celebration
Fair Activities: Temporary stalls; agricultural produce and daily-use articles are brought for sale.
Cultural Significance: Listed as an important fair in the district.

Historical Background: Listed among the other important fairs of Yavatmal District.
Rituals: Puja, abhishek, aarti, devotional singing, and prayers
Fair Activities: Temporary stalls; agricultural produce and daily-use articles are brought for sale.
Cultural Significance: Listed as an important fair in the district.

Historical Background: Mandir is believed to be “jagrut” (spiritually awakened), and practitioners believe heartfelt prayers made here are answered.
Rituals: Making vows (sankalp); visiting Mandir; returning the following year to offer thanks; pulling decorated bullock carts.
Fair Activities: Yatra gatherings; bullock-cart tradition; traditional music; yatris moving toward Mandir
Cultural Significance: Renowned across Washim district for its spiritual intensity and vow-centered rituals.

Alternate Name: Davha Yatra; Nath Nange Maharaj Yatra
Historical Background: Nathnange (Nagenath) Maharaj is described as a revered sant whose Samadhi is located at Shri Kshetra Dhawa.
Rituals: Religious rituals; kirtans; annual attendance considered a sacred vow by some participants.
Fair Activities: Fair/yatra gathering; religious and community activities.
Cultural Significance: Deeply rooted in local tradition and described as a major cultural and religious gathering.

Historical Background: Rituals; Shobhayatra; procession; judging decorated bullock pairs; children carrying miniature clay bull figures; dandiya and traditional instruments.
Rituals: Mahaprasad; refreshments
Fair Activities: Decorated bullock carts, dhol-tasha teams, lezim performers, bhajani mandals, children carrying clay bull figures, and prizes for decorated bullock pairs
Cultural Significance: Washim – Festivals & Fairs, last updated 22 July 2025

Duration: Annual; Kartika Vad 14 to Margashirsha Sud 2
Historical Background: Sakharam Maharaj Mandir was built in 1845. The sant is widely revered for fulfilling vows related to childbirth, employment, and health.
Rituals: Prayers; offerings after fulfillment of wishes; rath procession carrying sant's mask; palkhi; prakshal pida (ceremonial washing of sant's seat).
Fair Activities: Rath procession; palkhi; religious gathering
Cultural Significance: Major religious fair centred on Sant Sakharam Maharaj and vow fulfillment.

Historical Background: Shri Balaji is described as the gramdevta of Washim town.
Rituals: Kala Kirtan; Gopal Kala (Dahi Handi); grand procession; musicians narrating the life story of Shri Krishna.
Fair Activities: Grand procession; festive stalls; singing; decorations; cultural performances.
Cultural Significance: Combines religious rituals with cultural performances and reaffirms Shri Balaji's central role in Washim's spiritual and social life.

Historical Background: Mandir at the northern edge of Dhanora was built around 400 years ago using brick and lime mortar. The murti of Mahasiddha Buva is believed to be self-manifested.
Rituals: N/A
Fair Activities: N/A
Cultural Significance: Jatra dedicated to Shri Mahasiddha Buva.

Historical Background: According to locals, Sharif Sailani Shah arrived from Delhi and became known for curing individuals possessed by spirits. After his passing in 1908, the dargah was established and the urus has been observed annually.
Rituals: Incense burning; weekly rosewater washing on Fridays
Fair Activities: N/A
Cultural Significance: Annual urus associated with the dargah of Sharif Sailani Shah.

Historical Background: Buldhana district edition concluded on February 24, 2024. The event was intended to celebrate and promote Buldhana's cultural heritage.
Rituals: N/A
Fair Activities: Walkathon; 5 km and 3 km races; rangoli competition; bhajan competition; cultural activities
Cultural Significance: Platform to celebrate and promote the cultural heritage of Buldhana through music, art, and community involvement.

Historical Background: Celebrates the birth anniversary of Rajmata Jijau, born in Sindkhed Raja in 1598. Sindkhed Raja is described as her birthplace and a site of historical and cultural importance.
Rituals: Cultural play depicting the life of Shivaji Maharaj; adventure- and bravery-themed activities; horse competition
Fair Activities: Cultural performances; traditional competitions; community engagement; horse competition
Cultural Significance: Pays tribute to Rajmata Jijau's legacy and serves as a platform to celebrate Maratha heritage, culture, and valor.

Historical Background: Bhoi and Kumbhar communities celebrate Donkey Pola alongside the traditional Pola festival. Donkeys are described as important for transporting goods during the monsoon.
Rituals: Bathing donkeys; decorating them with flowers; honoring them through rituals.
Fair Activities: Community celebration associated with Pola.
Cultural Significance: Expression of gratitude and respect toward donkeys for their contribution to agricultural life.

Alternate Name: Dhargarh Yatra; Shri Kshetra Dhargad Yatra
Historical Background: Ancient Mandir at Sri Kshetra Dhargarh is located in the Satpura mountain range and houses two Swayambhu Shivlingams and a Nandi. The source notes that some people suggest Eklavya installed the Shivlingas.
Rituals: Chanting “Har Har Mahadev”; carrying Purna River water to Popatkhed; performing Jalabhishek on the Shivlinga; puja at the natural setting.
Fair Activities: Buses arranged from Akot; pilgrims travel from Akot toward Dhargarh; natural waterfall and Surya waterfall visited.
Cultural Significance: Religious pilgrimage centred on the Shivlingams at Sri Kshetra Dhargarh.

Historical Background: Bringing sacred water from Gandhigram/Purna River; carrying kavads; bringing palkhi; ceremonial ablution of the devta on the fourth Monday; receiving darshan at Rajrajeshwar Mandir.
Rituals: Sacred water from the Purna River
Fair Activities: Nearly a thousand young men carry the massive kavad; more than a thousand smaller kavads are mentioned.
Cultural Significance: Akola – Festivals & Fairs, last updated 18 July 2025

Village: Various villages and towns in Maharashtra
Religion: Hindu; Madia Indigenous tradition in specific communities
Deity: Devta Kodalpen (documented Madia tradition); otherwise Not Specified
Hindu Month: Shravana (Pithori Amavasya); some regional observances may fall in Bhadrapada
Duration: Generally 1 day; Marbat Mirvanuk occurs the following day in the documented Bhandara tradition
Historical Background: Celebrates bulls and oxen for their contribution to agriculture; regional traditions include Tanha Pola in Nagpur and distinct Madia practices in Gadchiroli.
Rituals: Bulls are bathed, decorated, worshipped and paraded. Children carry decorated wooden bulls during Tanha Pola. In the documented Madia tradition, rituals include worship of Kodalpen and feeding sacrificial bulls.
Fair Activities: Bull processions, children’s processions and local market activity; Marbat figures are paraded and burned the following day in the documented Bhandara tradition.
Cultural Significance: Expresses gratitude for bulls’ contribution to farming and preserves rural, regional and Indigenous traditions.
